grounding.states: short-term melatonin use appears safe for most people
grounding.from: The NIH says short-term melatonin use appears safe for most people

grounding.states: melatonin is typically safe and well tolerated at low doses, taken for the shortest time
grounding.from: UC Davis Health (Feb 2025) says melatonin is typically safe and well tolerated at low doses, taken appropriately for the shortest time.

grounding.states: short-term means one to two months
grounding.from: UC Davis defines short-term as one to two months.

grounding.states: adult doses are disputed: 0.3 to 1 mg per one doctor, 3 to 5 mg as the most common adult dose per GoodRx
grounding.from: Yale New Haven Health quotes a doctor saying adults should take only 0.3 to 1 mg, and not long-term. GoodRx says the most common adult dose is about 3 to 5 mg, taken 1 to 2 hours before bed.

grounding.states: a preliminary AHA abstract linked a year or more of use in chronic insomnia to higher heart failure rates: 4.6% of long-term users vs 2.7% of non-users over five years
grounding.from: An American Heart Association abstract was presented in November 2025. It reviewed records of 130,828 adults and found heart failure in 4.6% of long-term melatonin users versus 2.7% of non-users over five years.

grounding.states: the AHA study cannot prove cause and effect and is not yet peer-reviewed
grounding.from: The AHA says the study cannot prove cause and effect. The AHA also says the findings are preliminary because abstracts at its meetings are not peer-reviewed.

grounding.states: some experts think poor sleep may explain the results rather than melatonin
grounding.from: Scientific American reports that some experts think the results may reflect the effects of poor sleep rather than melatonin.

grounding.states: long-term sleep problems often point to an underlying condition that a doctor should look at
grounding.from: GoodRx also says long-term sleep problems often point to an underlying condition, and that taking melatonin long term without medical input could let that condition worsen.

value.answer: For most adults, short-term use looks fine. It's typically safe at low doses, taken for the shortest time you need, and UC Davis counts one to two months as short-term. The dose advice really does conflict, though, with some sources saying 0.3 to 1 mg and others 3 to 5 mg, so start at the low end. Taking it nightly for months is the part to be careful about. A preliminary AHA study from November 2025 linked a year or more of use in chronic insomnia to more heart failure (4.6% vs 2.7% over five years), but it isn't peer-reviewed yet, can't prove cause, and poor sleep may be the real driver. If you're thinking about using it long term, a doctor should look at why the sleep trouble keeps going.
